Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cryo-plasma FIB/SEM volume imaging of biological specimens" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Anna Akhmanova as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in the review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Alex de Marco (Reviewer #1); Alex J Noble (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) In its current form the paper does not show or discuss how plasma beams can mitigate charging artifacts (or not). The authors should add a comparison of charging artifacts with different sources (including Gallium) before computational correction. If this is not possible, they should remove the claim that they 'address these challenges using a cryogenic plasma FIB/SEM' (including charging). Similarly, the resolution measurements presented in the last supplementary figures do not relate to the use of plasma FIB/SEM in comparison with other beams.

2) Add a description of curtaining over time, in response to the following point from reviewer 1: "curtains appear over time when milling, and it would be useful to understand how different sources behave over time in FIB/SEM tomography sessions. The score is currently done from individual windows milled, which gives a good indication of the performance. However, it would make sense to check that the behaviour remains identical in an imaging setting and with the moving milling windows (or lines). This will show the counteracting effect to the redeposition and etching effect reported when imaging with the E-beam the milled face. "

3) Add data on milling resolution and beam cross-section in response to the following point from reviewer 1: "No detail about the milling resolution has been reported. Since different currents and beams have different cross-sections, it is expected to affect the z-resolution achievable during an imaging session. It would be useful to have a description of the beam cross-sections at the various conditions used and how or whether these interfere with the preparation."

4) Comment on the effects of imaging tilt angle on collection efficiency.

5) Explain the loss in resolution upon tilting the imaging angle, and the effect on contrast on the curtain edges (refer to reviewer 1 comment: "the generation of secondary electrons is known to increase with the increased tilt and to consider that the curtains (that are the prominent feature on the surface) are running along the tilt direction, it would be expected to see no contrast difference between the background and the edge of each curtain as the generation of secondary electrons will increase with tilt for both the edges and the background. Therefore, the contrast should be invariant, at least on the curtains").

6) Comment on reviewer 1 claim of suboptimal astigmatism correction, and on how this might affect the comparison between the different imaging tilt angles.

7) Discuss whether and how the contrast gained from the optimised approach using plasma FIB will allow interpretation and segmentation of biological features.

Can automated segmentation approaches be applied to the FIB/SEM volumes in similar ways to cryo-ET reconstructions?

Could the authors demonstrate that the features detected in the SEM can be used to target areas of interest for cryo-ET? If so, can they show structural preservation in the cryo-ET reconstructions?

Alternatively, the manuscript should more explicitly state that downstream correlative approaches are a potential application to be developed and tested in future work, and this is currently not possible.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

Suggestions for Improvement:

The results presented in this manuscript are substantial on their own, and merit publication. However, as written, I worry that most readers will have a similar experience as me, reading excitedly, on the edge of our seats, waiting for the proof-of-concept that this approach is effective (and perhaps more effective than CLEM) for targeting and downstream cryo-ET imaging, and will come up somewhat disappointed that this is not demonstrated.

I propose that the authors choose one of two possible paths to address the weakness above. The first, more extensive albeit thorough option, would be to address this by collecting tilt series data and reconstructing tomograms of the same lamella imaged by plasma cryo-FIB/SEM, and demonstrate that cross-correlation between volumetric cryo-FIB/SEM and cryo-ET acquisition is possible without affecting image/reconstruction quality. This could be evaluated either qualitatively (e.g. integrity of membranes/filaments) or structurally (e.g., by solving the subtomogram average of the cellular ribosome). Ideally, the authors would select a target and demonstrate an advantage of cryo-FIB/SEM targeting over the more standardized cryo-fluorescence/CLEM approaches.

The second option would be to revise the manuscript text to more explicitly state upfront that this work is solely focused on evaluating the performance of cryo-FIB/SEM for volumetric imaging and ultrastructural analyses, and that future work will determine whether these are of sufficient quality to the image by cryo-ET. The authors sort of dance around the possibility that this approach could be used for downstream applications without sufficiently testing this, and therefore, I believe the intent of the article needs to be more explicitly addressed in the manuscript text. This would strengthen the merits of the article by allowing the reader to focus on the substantial improvements to contrast/imaging without feeling like something is "missing" at the end.

Finally, I suggest that the authors apply an automated segmentation algorithm to their volumetric data as a more unbiased and practical metric to evaluate the degree to which cryo-FIB/SEM imaging increases resolution, contrast, and interpretability of subcellular features at scale that would enable biological insight.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors present a method for using the exceptional SEM imaging capabilities of the Helios Hydra and new cryo-plasma FIB milling functionality on vitrified biological specimens to obtain contextual information on cells and tissues while potentially localizing areas of interest for subsequent lamellae generation. Significant results are presented where analyses of the cryo-pFIB performance are qualitatively and quantitatively displayed and exemplified, which is particularly useful for the field as pFIBs begin to be used worldwide. The authors show SEM optimization examples from bacterial cells, mammalian cells, and tissue along with features that may be expected in the resolution range of the instrument (10 nm – 10 µm). The authors clearly compare the four plasma sources, proceed with the best source partly based on a proposed curtaining score, then optimize imaging quality by tilting to 90 degrees relative to the SEM, analyze several samples, and introduce a U-net algorithm for cleaning up charging streaks.

I have experience with cryo-FIB/SEM and cryo-ET/EM. Overall, I think this manuscript is timely and practical, given that cryo-pFIB/SEMs are anticipated to be adopted widely beginning in 2023, and should be published.

results.result: Argon and xenon plasma sources produce smoother surfaces with lower curtaining propensity (<10% at low currents) compared to nitrogen and oxygen, with argon showing superior performance at higher currents. Monatomic gases (Ar, Xe) produce single ion species avoiding double-image artifacts that occur with diatomic gases (N, O), which limited automated workflow success rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C22 provide converging experimental evidence from curtaining measurements, visual assessment, and operational observations. The curtaining propensity scores, double-image formation with diatomic gases, and workflow failure rates provide quantitative and qualitative support. C88 appropriately identifies this as speculation requiring further investigation.

results.result: Imaging perpendicular (90°) to the milled surface significantly improves image quality and resolution (47±7 nm) compared to 52° imaging (76±19 nm), with better contrast and reduced geometric distortion. The 52° angle causes geometric shortening by sin(α) resulting in ellipsoidal appearance of circular features.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 provide both qualitative visual assessment and quantitative FRC measurements demonstrating resolution improvement. Claims C71-C73 explain the geometric basis and show experimental validation through bacterial cell shape analysis. The combination of visual, quantitative, and geometric evidence strongly supports this result.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM of plunge-frozen HeLa cells (500 slices) visualized membranous organelles and identified two centrosomes with centriole pairs, with centrosome separation (~1.2 µm) and centriole spacing (543 nm and 1561 nm) consistent with prophase cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 provide direct observations from experimental data with measurements that align with cited literature values for prophase cells. The visualization of subcellular structures and quantitative measurements of centrosome/centriole spacing provide converging evidence, though the absence of spindle microtubules is noted.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM of mouse brain cortical tissue (844.4 µm³) revealed diverse cell types, myelinated neurons (diameter 0.53-2.8 µm), mitochondria (~87), and synaptic structures including pre-synaptic vesicles (20-30 nm diameter) with counts of ~184 and ~98 vesicles in two different synaptic terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 provide direct measurements and counts from experimental volumetric data. The range of observable structures from tissue-level organization to nanometer-scale vesicles demonstrates the technique's capability across scales. Quantitative measurements are specific and internally consistent.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM of R. rubrum (2.5 hr acquisition) visualized chromatophore formation including nascent chromatophores budding from the inner membrane, with 2772 mature and 84 nascent chromatophores identified across eight cells. One atypical cell showed ~12% nascent chromatophores while most had few or none, demonstrating the technique's ability to capture rare cellular events.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 and C69 provide direct experimental observations with specific counts. C68 claims novelty at this scale, and C95 appropriately infers the advantage for rare event detection. The measurements align with cited literature (C44, C70), and the uneven distribution observation (C46) is well-documented.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM of Vero cells identified 138 nuclear pore complexes, 26 LD-to-ER contacts, and 48 mitochondria-to-ER membrane contact sites, with both contact types showing similar volumes (1-5 × 10⁻³ µm³) and Gaussian distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 provide specific counts and volume measurements from experimental data. The similar volume distributions between different MCS types is quantitatively documented. However, the limited volume acquired (46 slices vs 500 for HeLa) due to nitrogen plasma issues (C22) may affect statistical robustness of these measurements.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM of fixed mouse heart tissue visualized sarcomere structures with average length 1.68 µm (likely post-mortem contraction) and quantified 997 mitochondria in 2698.4 µm³, yielding mitochondrial density of 0.36/µm³ (vs 0.10/µm³ in brain), consistent with literature values.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 provide direct measurements with good agreement to cited literature (C53, C96). C97 appropriately interprets the sarcomere length as post-mortem contraction rather than diastole based on comparison with in vivo values. The tissue fixation is noted, which may affect some ultrastructural features but allows quantitative comparisons.

results.result: Stage movement for 90° imaging introduces minimal drift (XY shift: 52±38 nm without movement, 96±71 nm with movement) and maintains accurate Z-step control (48.1±1.4 nm vs 50 nm target). Depth of field at 1-2 kV is ~20 µm, allowing ~400 slices before focus correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 provide quantitative measurements from bead experiments demonstrating the precision and stability of the imaging system. The XY drift increase with stage movement is modest (<1% of FOV), and Z-step accuracy is within 4% of target. Depth of field measurement provides practical guidance for automation.

results.result: Optimal SEM imaging parameters were empirically determined as 1.1-1.2 kV with 6.3-13 pA current, using 100 ns dwell time and 50-100 line integration for optimal contrast and minimal charging artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 report empirically optimized parameters from experimental work. While stated as 'in our hands,' these represent systematic optimization for the specific instrument and sample types. The parameters are specific and reproducible, though generalization to other systems may require re-optimization.

results.result: Plasma ion beam spot size characterization showed argon produces smallest probes at 30 kV, while at 20 kV all gases show similar spot sizes with argon/xenon plateauing early and nitrogen/oxygen increasing linearly with current.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 report direct measurements of beam profiles across different gases and voltages. The data provides important characterization for understanding milling resolution capabilities, though the absolute spot sizes are larger than Ga+ sources as expected.

results.result: No resolution degradation was observed during extended acquisitions (up to 500 slices). SEM electron dose was <10⁻² e⁻/Ų, with damage expected to be confined to <50 nm depth similar to FIB damage (~45 nm), both near the surface.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by FRC analysis throughout acquisition series. C56 provides dose calculations from experimental parameters. C57-C58 make reasonable inferences about damage depth based on electron interaction physics and cited literature, though C57 is explicitly stated as expectation rather than direct measurement.

results.result: Automated segmentation using machine learning (SuRVos2 for mitochondria, U-Net for charging centers) achieved high accuracy with Dice scores of 0.87 and 0.93 respectively, with volume percentages closely matching manual segmentation and minimal impact on image resolution after charge artifact removal.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 and C74-C76 provide quantitative validation metrics comparing automated to manual segmentation. Dice scores >0.85 indicate good agreement, and volume percentage agreement (24% vs 20%) supports practical utility. C75 appropriately suggests future full automation is feasible. C76 confirms charge removal preserves resolution.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM is compatible with correlative workflows, enabling correlation of subcellular features between SEM, TEM, and fluorescence imaging modalities on the same lamella, despite physical differences arising from imaging depth (SEM: ~25 nm surface vs TEM: full 300 nm thickness).
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C83-C84 demonstrate successful correlation across modalities with experimental data. C81-C82 correctly explain physical basis for observed differences. C85 draws appropriate conclusion about workflow compatibility. The differences between modalities are acknowledged and explained rather than being limitations.

results.result: Charging artifacts occur predominantly in lipid-rich regions (membranes, vesicles, myelin) and manifest as intense dark spots with asymmetric streaks along the scan direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 describe consistent observations across multiple samples (Figures 2-7). The association with lipid-rich regions is well-documented in the experimental data, and the morphological description of charging artifacts is specific and reproducible.

results.result: The automated workflow is relatively rapid with SEM imaging as the rate-limiting step (6-7 min) compared to milling (30 s for 20×4 µm with Ar), enabling complete datasets like R. rubrum in 2.5 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C59 and C104 provide specific timing measurements from experimental procedures. The identification of SEM as rate-limiting is important for future optimization. The 2.5 hr acquisition time (C43) demonstrates practical throughput for biological applications.

results.result: Curtaining propensity did not accumulate over time during automated acquisition. Higher curtaining was observed in tissue compared to cells, attributed to material heterogeneity (lumen, fascia, supportive layers milling at different rates), with protective layer composition and application affecting curtaining.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 reports direct observation of no temporal trends. C89 documents tissue vs cell differences with C90 providing reasonable mechanistic explanation based on material properties. C91 is supported by citation. However, C90 remains an attribution rather than experimentally validated mechanism.

results.result: Argon plasma milling at higher currents (200 pA at 20 kV for serial pFIB/SEM vs 50 pA at 30 kV for lamella polishing) may cause more damage than nitrogen, as nitrogen-milled Vero cells showed higher resolution than argon-milled HeLa cells, though prior work shows argon affects ribosome resolution within ~45 nm of surface.
results.evaluation: C77 cites prior work on argon damage. C78 correctly compares experimental parameters. However, C79's comparison between different cell types (Vero vs HeLa) with different plasma sources confounds cell type with plasma type, making it difficult to isolate the effect of plasma choice. The resolution difference could arise from multiple factors including sample preparation, cell type differences, or imaging parameters rather than solely plasma-induced damage.

results.result: The SEM electron interaction depth is estimated at 20-30 nm and varies by sample composition. No obvious vertical discontinuities from excessive electron dose were observed, with features successfully tracked across serial images.
results.evaluation: C92 is supported by citation to established literature. C93 correctly notes sample-dependent variation based on electron-matter interaction physics. C94 provides observational validation that the chosen 50 nm milling step and imaging parameters did not cause detectable damage artifacts in the experimental data.

results.result: The cryo-serial pFIB/SEM approach successfully produced 3D volumes of bacteria, cells, and tissue with 20-50 nm resolution using automated workflows. The technique is highly controllable, laboratory-based, and compatible with downstream imaging modalities, making it a useful addition to structural biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C101-C102 are directly supported by the range of experimental demonstrations across sample types. C103 is supported by precision measurements (C40-C41). C105 is inherent in using commercial equipment vs synchrotron. C106 is demonstrated by correlative imaging (C80-C85). C100 represents an appropriate summary conclusion based on the body of evidence.

results.result: The ability to visualize protein assemblies and ultrastructure in vitrified unstained tissue with laboratory equipment has potential applications in pathology for early disease mechanism identification.
results.evaluation: C98 summarizes demonstrated capabilities (visualization of NPCs, centrioles, synaptic vesicles in tissue). However, C99's claim about pathology applications is speculative. While the technical capability is demonstrated, translation to pathology would require validation on diseased tissue, development of disease-specific markers or features, and demonstration of diagnostic utility. No pathology samples were examined in this study.

results.result: Background and context claims establish that serial FIB/SEM enables mesoscale imaging (10 nm-10 µm), vitrified samples preserve hydration for downstream cryo-ET, but face challenges of low contrast, curtaining, and charging. Plasma FIB sources offer higher currents than Ga+ for tissue milling, while imaging at crossover energies reduces charging in insulating biological materials.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C13, C62-C67) establish the scientific context and are supported by established knowledge and appropriate citations. They correctly describe the state of the field, technical requirements, and known limitations that motivate the current work. These are primarily literature-based knowledge claims rather than novel findings.

results.result: The authors compared four plasma sources (argon, xenon, nitrogen, oxygen) for cryo-FIB/SEM imaging, finding that argon and xenon produce the smoothest surfaces with lowest curtaining propensity (<10% at low currents), while nitrogen and oxygen produce double images due to multiple ion species that interfere with automated workflows.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this work as providing 'significant results' where 'analyses of the cryo-pFIB performance are qualitatively and quantitatively displayed and exemplified, which is particularly useful for the field.' The comparison of plasma sources and curtaining score is noted as a key contribution, with reviewers requesting additional data on curtaining over time rather than challenging the findings.

results.result: During automated serial pFIB/SEM imaging, no trends in curtain accumulation or changes in curtaining propensity over time were observed.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically requests 'a description of curtaining over time' noting that 'curtains appear over time when milling, and it would be useful to understand how different sources behave over time in FIB/SEM tomography sessions.' This indicates the reviewers found the evidence on temporal curtaining behavior insufficient.

results.result: Imaging at 90° to the milled surface provides significantly better contrast and resolution (47±7 nm) compared to 52° imaging (76±19 nm), with features appearing more prominent and geometrically accurate at 90°.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the optimization work, Reviewer 1 raises concerns about the explanation for resolution loss at tilted angles and questions the contrast differences on curtain edges, stating 'it would be expected to see no contrast difference between the background and the edge of each curtain.' Additionally, Reviewer 1 claims 'suboptimal astigmatism correction' may affect the comparison, requiring the authors to 'comment on how this might affect the comparison between the different imaging tilt angles.'

results.result: Optimal SEM imaging parameters were determined to be 1.1-1.2 kV with 6.3-13 pA current, using 100 ns dwell time and 50-100 line integration for best contrast and minimal charging.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the authors 'provide several recommendations for imaging conditions' and describe this as useful practical guidance. The optimization is acknowledged as part of the substantial methodological contribution without specific critique.

results.result: In plunge-frozen HeLa cells, various membranous compartments were clearly visualized including nucleus, ER, mitochondria, and two centrosomes with centrioles, with measurements consistent with cells in prophase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the authors 'show SEM optimization examples from bacterial cells, mammalian cells, and tissue along with features that may be expected in the resolution range of the instrument (10 nm – 10 µm).' These cellular observations are accepted as demonstrating the technique's capabilities.

results.result: In mouse brain cortical tissue, a volume of 844.4 μm³ was imaged revealing myelinated neurons, mitochondria with cristae, and synaptic junctions with pre-synaptic vesicles (20-30 nm diameter), with vesicle counts of ~184 and ~98 in two different synapses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the authors demonstrate imaging across sample types including tissue, and these observations are part of the accepted demonstration that the approach 'can accurately determine biological ultrastructural arrangements from simple bacteria to complex tissue.' No specific concerns are raised about these measurements.

results.result: In R. rubrum bacteria, both mature (30-60 nm diameter) and nascent chromatophores were observed, with nascent chromatophores budding from the inner membrane visualized at a scale not previously achieved, enabled by the ability to image large volumes quickly.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the biological observations across different sample types. The claim about novelty of visualization scale is accepted without challenge, and the rapid volumetric imaging capability is recognized as an advantage of the technique.

results.result: In Vero cells, 138 nuclear pore complexes were observed, along with 26 lipid droplet-to-ER contacts and 48 mitochondria-to-ER membrane contact sites, with both types of contacts having similar volumes (1-5 × 10⁻³ μm³).
results.evaluation: These observations are part of the accepted demonstration of subcellular feature visualization. Reviewers do not challenge these specific counts or measurements, accepting them as examples of the technique's capability to reveal cellular organization.

results.result: In heart tissue, sarcomere structures were visible with average length 1.68 μm (likely post-mortem contracted), and 997 mitochondria were counted in 2698.4 μm³, giving a mitochondrial concentration of 0.36/μm³ (vs 0.10/μm³ in brain), consistent with literature values.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these quantitative measurements as demonstrating the technique's utility. The comparison with literature values and between tissue types is not challenged, supporting the claim that the approach enables 'accurate assessment of the mitochondrial density in this tissue and quantitative comparison with the brain tissue.'

results.result: Precision measurements showed XY shift of 52±38 nm without stage movement (96±71 nm with movement), milling step accuracy of 48.1±1.4 nm for targeted 50 nm steps, and depth of field of ~20 μm at 1-2 kV.
results.evaluation: These technical characterization measurements are accepted as part of the methodological validation. Reviewers do not challenge these precision metrics, which support the claim that the approach is 'highly controllable.'

results.result: No resolution degradation was observed during extended acquisitions (500 slices), with SEM dose under 10⁻² e⁻/Ų, and damage expected to be confined to <50 nm depth similar to FIB damage (~45 nm), with no obvious discontinuities from excessive electron dose.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these damage and stability assessments. The lack of resolution degradation over time supports the technique's viability for extended imaging sessions, which is implicitly accepted in the overall positive evaluation.

results.result: Automated segmentation of mitochondria achieved a Dice score of 0.87 compared to manual segmentation, with volume percentages in agreement (24% vs 20%), and charge center segmentation achieved 0.93 Dice score indicating minimal manual cleanup needed.
results.evaluation: While these segmentation results are presented, Reviewer 2 specifically requests that 'the authors apply an automated segmentation algorithm to their volumetric data as a more unbiased and practical metric to evaluate the degree to which cryo-FIB/SEM imaging increases resolution, contrast, and interpretability of subcellular features at scale.' This suggests reviewers want more extensive demonstration that automated approaches can be applied effectively, questioning whether current results sufficiently prove biological interpretability.

results.result: Correlative imaging demonstrated that subcellular structures could be correlated between SEM and TEM images of the same lamella, photosynthetic vesicles in R. rubrum were straightforward to correlate, and chlorophyll fluorescence could be correlated with both pFIB/SEM and TEM, supporting suitability for correlative workflows.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise significant concerns about downstream applications. Reviewer 2 states readers will 'come up somewhat disappointed that this is not demonstrated' regarding proof-of-concept for targeting and cryo-ET. The essential revision requests that authors either 'demonstrate that cross-correlation between volumetric cryo-FIB/SEM and cryo-ET acquisition is possible without affecting image/reconstruction quality' or 'more explicitly state upfront that this work is solely focused on evaluating the performance of cryo-FIB/SEM for volumetric imaging' and that correlative approaches are 'currently not possible.'

results.result: Charging artifacts occur in lipid-rich regions manifesting as dark spots with asymmetric streaks, but can be computationally removed while maintaining overall image resolution.
results.evaluation: Essential revision 1 states 'the paper does not show or discuss how plasma beams can mitigate charging artifacts (or not)' and requests 'a comparison of charging artifacts with different sources (including Gallium) before computational correction.' Reviewers indicate the claim that plasma FIB/SEM addresses charging challenges is not adequately supported, requiring either additional data or removal of this claim.

results.result: The cryo-plasma FIB/SEM approach produced 3D volumes of bacteria, cells, and tissue with 20-50 nm resolution, is highly controllable, relatively rapid, laboratory-based, and compatible with subsequent imaging modalities, making it a useful addition to the structural biology toolbox.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state this is 'important work' that 'should be very useful for addressing many biological questions' and that 'the results presented in this manuscript are substantial on their own, and merit publication.' The overall capabilities and advantages are accepted, though specific applications require further validation.

results.result: At 30 kV, argon produced the smallest probe sizes, while at 20 kV all sources showed similar spot sizes with argon and xenon plateauing early while oxygen and nitrogen increased linearly.
results.evaluation: Essential revision 3 requests 'data on milling resolution and beam cross-section' noting 'No detail about the milling resolution has been reported. Since different currents and beams have different cross-sections, it is expected to affect the z-resolution achievable.' This indicates reviewers found the beam characterization incomplete for assessing its impact on imaging performance.

results.result: Comparison of Vero cells milled with nitrogen plasma versus HeLa cells milled with argon plasma showed nitrogen produced higher resolution images.
results.evaluation: This finding appears to contradict the main conclusion favoring argon, and reviewers' request for comparison of charging artifacts with different sources (essential revision 1) suggests they want more systematic comparison data. The limited comparison presented is insufficient to draw firm conclusions about relative performance.

results.result: Serial FIB/SEM on vitrified samples can target structures while maintaining hydration for downstream cryo-ET, which requires thin lamellae (<300 nm). Plasma FIB sources operate at higher currents than Ga+ and may reduce ion implantation, addressing limitations of cryo-fluorescence microscopy's poor axial resolution (>300 nm).
results.evaluation: These contextual and technical background claims about the motivation for the work are accepted by reviewers without challenge. The reviewers acknowledge the field has 'long searched for a suitable method to combine the pristine preservation of vitrified samples with a volumetric imaging modality,' validating the problem statement.

Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, requesting additional 'data on milling resolution and beam cross-section' to assess impact on z-resolution, finding characterization incomplete.

Both evaluate correlative imaging claims (C80-C85). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding successful correlation and appropriate conclusions about workflow compatibility. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting readers will be 'disappointed' and requiring either demonstration of cryo-ET correlation or explicit statement that it's 'currently not possible.'

Both address charging artifacts (C86-C87, C3, C76). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with consistent observations across samples. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating paper 'does not show or discuss how plasma beams can mitigate charging artifacts' and requesting comparison with different sources including Gallium before computational correction.

Both evaluate overall capabilities and advantages (C4, C100-C106). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on range of experimental demonstrations. Peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED, calling this 'important work' with 'substantial' results meriting publication, though noting specific applications require further validation.

Both evaluate argon vs nitrogen comparison (C77-C79). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting confounding of cell type with plasma type makes isolating plasma effect difficult. Peer reviewers also rate as UNCERTAIN, requesting more systematic comparison data as this finding appears to contradict main conclusion favoring argon.

Both evaluate contextual and background claims (C1-C13, C62-C67 for OpenEval; C2, C5-C10 for peer). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these are literature-based knowledge claims. Peer reviewers accept problem statement without challenge, acknowledging the field motivation.

OpenEval evaluates timing measurements (C59, C104) as SUPPORTED, identifying SEM as rate-limiting and noting practical throughput. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these timing claims.
